A. Awards
The Petitioner argues that SCOPS "improperly discounted testimonial evidence from .I.. .____.
medalists and national champions who credited [the Beneficiary's] coaching for their achievements."
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o )(3)(iii)(B)(]) requires "[d ]ocumentation of the alien's receipt of
nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence in the field of endeavor."
( emphasis added). USCIS determines whether the person was the recipient of prizes or awards in the
field of endeavor.3 A person may rely on a team award, provided the person is one of the recipients
of the award. 4

Here, the Petitioner claims the Beneficiary's eligibility based on awards or prizes won by his students,
some of which received various awards after the Beneficiary's tenure as their coach. Although the
Petitioner presented letters from individuals who were coached by the Beneficiary and credited him
for being impactfol in their athletic accomplishments, the Petitioner did not establish that the
Beneficiary received nationally or internationally recognized prizes or awards for excellence in the
field. Without evidence showing that the Beneficiary actually acquired those prizes or awards, the
submission of evidence reflecting prizes or awards obtained by others is not sufficient to meet this
criterion.
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

B. Judging
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(4) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's participation on
a panel, or individually, as a judge of the work of others in the same or in an allied field of
specialization to that for which classification is sought." USCIS determines whether the person has
acted as the judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specialization. 5
As indicated in SCOPS' decision the Petitioner initiall claimed that the Beneficiary was appointed

participated as a judge to evaluate the works of others," and the "evidence suggest[ ed] that the
beneficiary was employed as a Director in an advisory role to train students at a training camp which
[was] more akin to a coach, rather than being invited as a judge to evaluate works of others." In
response to the request for evidence, the Petitioner presented a letter from the Beneficiary asserting
his participation in various juries. However, the Petitioner did not support the record with evidence
corroborating any of the Beneficiary's claims.
For the reasons discussed in SCOPS' decision, we agree that the Petitioner did not demonstrate the
Beneficiary participated as a judge of the work of others consistent with this regulatory criterion, and
the Petitioner did not provide evidence supporting the Beneficiary's assertions in his self-serving
letter. 6

Although the Petitioner claims the Beneficiary's eligibility for an additional criterion on appeal
(original contributions under 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(0 )(3)(iii)(B)(5)), we need not reach this ground because
the Beneficiary cannot fulfill the initial evidentiary requirement of at least three under 8 C.F.R.
